### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, about 98 in 100 outgoing transitions of A25 went to A27; in the later window, A25's outgoing transitions split almost evenly across A35, A36 and A41 (about 31–33 in 100 each), with A27 as a direct target nearly gone (about 0.5 in 100). [DIR001]
- A26's outgoing routing flipped from a three-way split over A41, A35 and A36 (about 38, 33 and 28 in 100) to almost exclusively A30 (about 98 in 100). [DIR002]
- The block A35/A36/A41 previously routed among its members and exited to A30 (about 28–34 in 100 per member); in the later window it exits predominantly to A27 (about 30–33 in 100 per member), and A30 is essentially no longer reached from it. [DIR003, DIR004, DIR005]
- All six measured orderings between {A26, A27} and {A35, A36, A41} reversed: before, A26 or A27 came first in about 98–100 in 100 cases; in the later window the trio member comes first in about 97–98 in 100, while the two activities still co-occur in every trace (200 of 200 in both windows). [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006]
- Relative event positions moved consistently: A35, A36 and A41 now occur earlier (mean position about 0.58 to about 0.42 of the trace), while A27 (about 0.38 to 0.47) and A26 (about 0.53 to 0.62) occur later. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005]
- Step distances changed accordingly: A25 and A27, previously one step apart in about 98 in 100 cases, are now about 4–5 steps apart (about 90 in 100 at four steps); A26 and A30, previously about 4–5 steps apart, are now one step apart in about 98 in 100 cases. [LAG001, LAG003]
- Further lag changes (for A25–A35, A26 with A35/A36/A41, and the trio towards A30) point the same way but rest on only 1–2 observations in one window and are weak individually. [LAG002, LAG004, LAG005, LAG006, LAG007, LAG008, LAG009, LAG010]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that the routing block A35/A36/A41 and the segment containing A27 and A26 exchanged their places: the earlier window is consistent with A25 followed immediately by A27, then A26, then the A35/A36/A41 block exiting to A30, while in the later window A25 feeds into the A35/A36/A41 block, which leads to A27, with A26 following later and flowing directly into A30. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005, REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006, LAG001, LAG003, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005]

The support is direct and coherent: the relational items show the order between each of A26/A27 and each of A35/A36/A41 reversed while co-occurrence stayed complete; the adjacency items show A25 losing its direct step to A27 and A26 gaining a direct step to A30; and the routing and positional shifts match the same rearrangement, with each core item resting on essentially all 200 traces per window. The 26 qualifying items are many times the roughly 0.63 expected for an unchanged process, so the pattern as a whole is not what random re-splits produce. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005, REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006, LAG001, LAG003, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005]

Limitations: the evidence contains no outgoing routing profile for A27 or A30 and nothing on what precedes A26, so parts of the connective detail (what now follows A27, what feeds A26) are inferred from the partner activities rather than observed directly. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005] Several lag items rest on only 1–2 observations in one window, showing that rare variants do surface in a single window, so sampling differences in variant frequencies remain a competing explanation for those individual items — though they cannot plausibly account for the near-deterministic reversal of all six orderings at this sample size; the agreeing items also largely describe one underlying rearrangement rather than independent confirmations, and the positional shifts are event positions used only as corroboration. [LAG002, LAG004, LAG005, LAG006, LAG007, LAG008, LAG009, LAG010]
